name: Omkar and Landslide
description: Omkar is standing at the foot of Celeste mountain. The summit is $$$n$$$ meters away from him, and he can see all of the mountains up to the summit, so for all $$$1 \leq j \leq n$$$ he knows that the height of the mountain at the point $$$j$$$ meters away from himself is $$$h_j$$$ meters. It turns out that for all $$$j$$$ satisfying $$$1 \leq j \leq n - 1$$$, $$$h_j \lt h_{j + 1}$$$ (meaning that heights are strictly increasing). Suddenly, a landslide occurs! While the landslide is occurring, the following occurs: every minute, if $$$h_j + 2 \leq h_{j + 1}$$$, then one square meter of dirt will slide from position $$$j + 1$$$ to position $$$j$$$, so that $$$h_{j + 1}$$$ is decreased by $$$1$$$ and $$$h_j$$$ is increased by $$$1$$$. These changes occur simultaneously, so for example, if $$$h_j + 2 \leq h_{j + 1}$$$ and $$$h_{j + 1} + 2 \leq h_{j + 2}$$$ for some $$$j$$$, then $$$h_j$$$ will be increased by $$$1$$$, $$$h_{j + 2}$$$ will be decreased by $$$1$$$, and $$$h_{j + 1}$$$ will be both increased and decreased by $$$1$$$, meaning that in effect $$$h_{j + 1}$$$ is unchanged during that minute. The landslide ends when there is no $$$j$$$ such that $$$h_j + 2 \leq h_{j + 1}$$$. Help Omkar figure out what the values of $$$h_1, \dots, h_n$$$ will be after the landslide ends. It can be proven that under the given constraints, the landslide will always end in finitely many minutes. Note that because of the large amount of input, it is recommended that your code uses fast IO.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^6$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$h_1, h_2, \dots, h_n$$$ satisfying $$$0 \leq h_1 \lt h_2 \lt \dots \lt h_n \leq 10^{12}$$$ — the heights.
output_specification: Output $$$n$$$ integers, where the $$$j$$$-th integer is the value of $$$h_j$$$ after the landslide has stopped.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1392F — Omkar and Landslide [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
